entries.title: Primality testing: trial division vs AKS

algorithms.name: trial division
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(sqrt(N)) = Theta(2^(n/2)) divisions in the worst case (N prime): exactly 1 + floor((floor(sqrt N) - 1)/2) divisions on an odd prime N and at most that many on any N >= 2; n-bit primes exist for every n >= 2 (Bertrand's postulate, proved in PROOFS.md)

algorithms.name: AKS
algorithms.time_complexity: Õ(n^(21/2)) bit operations when multiplication and division of m-bit integers cost Õ(m), and O(n^(33/2)) with schoolbook integer arithmetic: polynomial, for this implementation. On every n-bit prime with n >= 24 it performs at least (n - 1)^4 n coefficient operations (Omega(n^5)). Faster analyses and the Lenstra-Pomerance variant: see background.

entries.title: Assignment problem: permutation enumeration vs the Hungarian method

algorithms.name: permutation enumeration
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n * n!) under the machine-model assumption on itertools.permutations listed under background, and Omega(n * n!) unconditionally: n! permutations, Theta(n) to cost each, exactly n * n! matrix reads on every input (PROOFS.md section 1)

algorithms.name: Hungarian method (shortest augmenting paths with potentials)
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n^3) worst case: the search for the i-th inserted row runs at most i iterations of its main loop, because every iteration except the last selects a column that is already matched (the loop stops at the first free column selected), the selected columns are distinct, and only i - 1 columns are matched at that time; iteration t evaluates one reduced cost for each of the n - t + 1 columns not yet selected and does Theta(n) further work. Hence at most n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 reduced-cost evaluations and O(n^3) time on every input (PROOFS.md Lemma H0). Theta(n^3) growth measured on the column-dominant family used for timing (no proof of that lower bound is given here)

entries.title: Powering in non-associative Cayley-Dickson algebras (octonions, sedenions, dimension 32): repeated multiplication vs square-and-multiply

algorithms.name: repeated multiplication
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(e) = Theta(2^n) algebra products: exactly e - 1 of them (and e - 1 >= 2^(n-1) - 1), i.e. (e - 1) 4^m multiplications of residues (PROOFS.md, sections 1 and 2); the loop control of range(e - 1) is not counted

algorithms.name: left-to-right square-and-multiply (binary method)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n) algebra products: exactly floor(log2 e) + popcount(e) - 1 <= 2(n - 1) of them (n - 1 squarings and popcount(e) - 1 multiplications by x), i.e. that many times 4^m residue multiplications (PROOFS.md, section 3); reading the bits of e with bin(e) takes Theta(n) under the machine-model assumption in background (PROOFS.md, section 10)

bases: Biss, D. K.; Dugger, D.; Isaksen, D. C. (2008). Large annihilators in Cayley-Dickson algebras. Communications in Algebra 36(2), 632-664, doi:10.1080/00927870701724094: Definition 2.1, Section 2 and Lemma 3.6, the identities x + x* = 2Re(x) and x x* = x* x = ||x||^2, from which power-associativity follows in a few lines (PROOFS.md, section 5).

Etherington, I. M. H. (1941). Some non-associative algebras in which the multiplication of indices is commutative. Journal of the London Mathematical Society 16, 48-55, doi:10.1112/jlms/s1-16.1.48, pp. 50-51: in a non-associative linear algebra where every element satisfies a quadratic equation, multiplication is associative for powers (stated without proof).

Schafer, R. D. (1961). An Introduction to Nonassociative Algebras, lecture notes (Project Gutenberg #25156), Chapter III, (25)-(31): the 2^t-dimensional algebras of the Cayley-Dickson process are quadratic, x^2 - t(x)x + n(x)1 = 0 (with a different doubling convention).
The binary method (Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 2, Section 4.6.3).
provenance.note: Credit only: every claim of the entry is proved in PROOFS.md (Lemma 1 over any commutative ring, power-associativity, correctness and exact counts of both algorithms, the non-associativity witnesses). Power-associativity of algebras in which every element satisfies a quadratic equation is stated, without proof, by Etherington (1941), and Schafer's 1961 lecture notes show that the Cayley-Dickson algebras are quadratic, under a different doubling convention; the proof here is our own and derives power-associativity from the identities of Biss, Dugger and Isaksen in a few lines. Schafer (1954) was not read.

entries.title: Determinant over GF(p): cofactor expansion vs Gaussian elimination

algorithms.name: Laplace (cofactor) expansion
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n!) field operations (n!/k! recursion nodes with k columns left, Theta(k^2) work each; n! * sum_k k^2/k! = Theta(n!)); exactly floor(e n!) - 1 multiplications for n >= 1 (PROOFS.md section 1)

algorithms.name: Gaussian elimination mod p
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) field operations on non-singular input: exactly (n^3 - n)/3 multiply-subtracts (~n^3/3), n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 multiplications in all and n inversions (PROOFS.md section 2); O(n^3) always (it can stop early on a singular matrix)

entries.title: Edit (Levenshtein) distance: plain recursion vs Wagner-Fischer DP

lower_bounds.bound: no O(n^(2-eps)) algorithm for any eps > 0
lower_bounds.setting: conditional on the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH)
lower_bounds.source: Backurs & Indyk 2015, main result (background: cited, conditional, not proved in this entry)

algorithms.name: plain recursion
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(D(n, n)) = Theta((3 + 2 sqrt 2)^n / sqrt(n)) (3 + 2 sqrt 2 = 5.83 to two decimals), D = Delannoy numbers: the calls d(i, j) with i = n or j = n are the leaves, and the root-to-leaf paths are the lattice paths from (0, 0) with steps (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1) stopped at their first point with i = n or j = n; each extends in exactly one way to (n, n), so there are D(n, n) leaves, and since every other call has 3 children the recursion makes exactly (3 D(n, n) - 1)/2 calls. D(n, n) = sum_k C(n, k)^2 2^k = Theta((3 + 2 sqrt 2)^n / sqrt(n)): by Stirling its largest term, near k = (2 - sqrt 2) n, is Theta((3 + 2 sqrt 2)^n / n), and summing the Theta(sqrt n) terms around it gives the 1/sqrt(n) factor; PROOFS.md section 3 proves all of this with explicit constants (3 * 10^-4 <= D(n, n) sqrt(n) / (3 + 2 sqrt 2)^n <= 6 for n >= 1)

algorithms.name: Wagner-Fischer dynamic programming
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2): exactly |a| |b| inner iterations and |a| + 1 rows of length |b| + 1 (Theta(|a| |b|) for non-empty strings)

entries.title: Fibonacci numbers: naive recursion vs dynamic programming vs fast doubling

algorithms.name: naive recursion
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(phi^n), phi = (1+sqrt(5))/2 ~ 1.618

algorithms.name: bottom-up dynamic programming
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n) word operations: exactly n loop iterations (range iteration at O(1) per step: machine-model assumption in background)

algorithms.name: fast doubling (matrix power)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(log n) word operations: exactly n.bit_length() loop iterations (n >= 1), with bin(n) built in O(log n) (machine-model assumption in background)

entries.title: Greatest common divisor: trial divisors vs Euclid's algorithm

algorithms.name: trial divisors
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(2^n) iterations in the worst case: for a, b >= 1 exactly min(a, b) - gcd(a, b) + 1 iterations of one or two divisions (none if a = 0 or b = 0); for n >= 2 the maximum over inputs with max(a, b) of bit length n is 2^n - 2, attained by the coprime pair (2^n - 1, 2^n - 2); the coprime Fibonacci pairs used for V2 need F_k >= 2^n / 3 > 2^(n-2) iterations (the pair is F_(k+1), F_k with F_(k+1) < 2^n <= F_(k+2), and F_(k+2) = F_(k+1) + F_k <= 3 F_k). In bit operations: at most 2^n iterations with at most two divisions of numbers below 2^n each, i.e. O(2^n n^2) with schoolbook division.

algorithms.name: Euclid's algorithm
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n) division steps: at most log_phi(min(a, b)) + 2 < 1.4405 n + 2 if min(a, b) >= 1, and at most one step otherwise (after Lamé 1844; PROOFS.md section 5). Consecutive Fibonacci numbers are the worst case: the smallest pair a > b >= 1 that needs k steps is (F_(k+2), F_(k+1)), and the V2 pair (F_(k+1), F_k) needs k - 1 = 1.44 n + O(1) steps for n >= 2. O(n^2) bit operations with schoolbook division: a step with quotient q on numbers below 2^n costs O(n (1 + log2 max(q, 1))), and the quotients q >= 1 multiply to at most max(a, b) < 2^n; Theta(n^2) on the Fibonacci pairs, where the step dividing F_(j+1) by F_j reads at least (j - 1) log2(phi) bits.

entries.title: Global minimum cut: all bipartitions vs Stoer-Wagner

algorithms.name: brute force
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2 2^n): exactly n(n-1)2^(n-3) weight additions and 2^(n-1) - 2 weight comparisons (n >= 2), plus Theta(n) other work per subset (PROOFS.md, sections 1 and 6). In terms of the input size N = n^2 entries this is 2^Theta(sqrt(N)), still super-polynomial.

algorithms.name: Stoer-Wagner (array)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) with plain arrays (each access to the dictionary key counted as one word operation): a phase on k vertices costs Theta(k^2); exactly (n-1)(n-2)(n+3)/6 weight additions and n(n-1)(n-2)/6 + n - 2 weight comparisons (n >= 2) (PROOFS.md, sections 2 and 6).

entries.title: Horn-SAT: brute force over all assignments vs linear-time unit propagation

algorithms.name: brute force over all assignments
algorithms.time_complexity: O(2^n * (L + 1)) always; Theta(2^n * n) = Theta(2^n * m) on the V2 family H_n, where every assignment is examined (unsatisfiable) and the 2^(n-1) assignments with x1 false pass n - 2 clauses before failing: exactly (2n + 13) 2^(n-2) - 2n - 4 literal evaluations.

algorithms.name: unit propagation with clause counters (Dowling-Gallier)
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n + L + 1) on every input: every variable is set true at most once, so every negative literal occurrence is decremented at most once and every clause fires at most once. Theta(n + L) on every input without an empty clause, since the build pass then reads every literal; at an empty clause the build pass stops at once. On H_n exactly 12n - 7 counted operations.

algorithms.name: dynamic programming
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2): exactly |a| |b| inner iterations and |a| + 1 rows of length |b| + 1 (Theta(|a| |b|) for non-empty strings)

entries.title: Longest increasing subsequence: subset enumeration vs quadratic DP vs patience sorting

algorithms.name: subset enumeration
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(2^n n) on every input (each of the 2^n masks is scanned over all n positions, with no early exit)

algorithms.name: quadratic dynamic programming
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) on every input: n(n-1)/2 comparisons

algorithms.name: patience sorting with binary search
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n (1 + log L)) <= O(n log n) for n >= 2, L = the answer (at most n (1 + log2 L) comparisons); Theta(n log n) in the worst case, e.g. on increasing input (L = n), which is the V2 scaling input; not Theta(n log L) on every input (PROOFS.md section 7)

entries.title: Optimal LZ77-style parsing with k repeat-offset slots: enumeration of all parses vs dynamic programming over (position, slot contents)

algorithms.name: enumeration of all parses
algorithms.time_complexity: 2^Theta(n log n) token evaluations in the worst case, for every fixed k >= 1 and REPMIN >= 1 (a token evaluation = one extension of a partial parse by one token, i.e. one edge of the search tree). Lower bound (PROOFS.md 6.4): on F1(m) = x_1 a b x_2 a b ... x_m a b (x_j fresh), block j >= 2 can be coded by two literals or by a new match of length 2 at any of the distances 3, 6, ..., 3(j-1), so there are at least m! parses, i.e. at least floor(n/3)! = 2^((1/3 - o(1)) n log2 n) evaluations for n >= 1 after padding with fresh symbols. Upper bound, for n >= 1 (PROOFS.md 6.5): a parse is a composition of n into token lengths (2^(n-1) choices) with at most n + k + 1 tokens of each length at each position, so there are at most 2^(n-1) (n + k + 1)^n parses; a partial parse is determined by the complete parse obtained by appending literals and by its number of tokens, so there are at most (n + 1) 2^(n-1) (n + k + 1)^n search-tree nodes. Besides the evaluations, the search does O((n + k)(E + 1)) elementary operations for E evaluations, plus Theta(n^2) for the match-length table (PROOFS.md 6.6), so its time is also 2^Theta(n log n) in the worst case. Exactly sum_{j=1}^{m} (j-1)! (j+2) = m! (1 + 3/m + O(1/m^2)) token evaluations on the V2 family (n = 3m, REPMIN = 3, any k), with exactly m! complete parses (PROOFS.md section 2).

algorithms.name: dynamic programming over (position, slot contents)
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n^(k+2)) relaxations for every input and fixed k, plus Theta(n^2) for the match-length table (a relaxation = one candidate value offered to a successor state). Proof (PROOFS.md 6.2): a slot value is 1 or the distance d <= i - 2 of an earlier new match, so position i has at most n^k states and at most n^(k-1) prefix groups; every token at position i has length at most n - i, so a state makes at most 1 + k(n - i) relaxations and a group at most i (n - i); the total over the n positions is at most n [n^k (1 + kn) + n^(k-1) n^2] = O(n^(k+2)). Besides the relaxations the DP does O(k T + n^2) elementary operations for T relaxations (PROOFS.md 6.3), so its time is O(n^(k+2)) for fixed k and n >= 1. The bound is tight: on a^n the DP has at least sum_{i=2k+1}^{n} prod_{t=1}^{k} (i - 2t) = n^(k+1)/(k+1) - O(n^k) states and makes n^(k+2)/(k+2) + O(n^(k+1)) relaxations, and every input has at most 3 + sum_{j=1}^{n-2} j^k states, for every REPMIN >= 1 (theorems/lz77-repeat-slots-state-bounds, Theorem C; that note is labelled undetermined). Exactly (4m^3 - 15m^2 + 29m - 9)/3 relaxations on the V2 family (k = 2, REPMIN = 3, n = 3m; PROOFS.md section 3).

bases: Bloom 2015, blog post '01-23-15 - LZA New Optimal Parse' (folklore, not peer-reviewed)
provenance.note: The DP itself is folklore (Bloom's blog, not peer-reviewed; see background). entries.title: Maximum-weight independent set on k x n grids with diagonals: exhaustive search vs DP over a path decomposition

algorithms.name: exhaustive search over all vertex subsets
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(N 2^N) on every input with N = k n >= 1 under the background sort assumption (needed only for the final sorted() of the output), i.e. 2^Theta(n) for every fixed k (N-bit masks as words; the final sorted() of at most N output vertices is O(N log N) under the background sort assumption; PROOFS.md, section 5). Exactly N 2^(N-1) weight additions on every input: (3/2) n 8^n for k = 3 (the V2 family; PROOFS.md, section 1).

algorithms.name: DP over the columns (path decomposition of width 2k-1)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(F_{k+2}^2 n) = Theta(phi^(2k) n) word operations for n >= 2 apart from sorting the output set, O(F_{k+2}^2) for n = 1 (F_{k+2}^2 compatibility tests per column; F_{k+2} = 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 for k = 1..6). The final sorted() of the at most n ceil(k/2) chosen vertices adds O(n k log(n k)) under the background sort assumption. So for every fixed k: Theta(n) apart from that sort, O(n log n) with it; exponential in k (PROOFS.md, section 6). Weight additions: exactly n P_k + (n-1) F_{k+2} on every instance with n >= 1 and positive weights (with zero weights, exactly z fewer, z = the number of c in 1..n-1 such that columns 0..c-1 have only zero weights; PROOFS.md, section 2), where P_k is the total number of rows over all column states; 10n - 5 for k = 3 (P_3 = 5, F_5 = 5), the V2 family.

algorithms.name: enumeration of all (n-1)-edge subsets
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n * C(n(n-1)/2, n-1)) = 2^Theta(n log n) under the background assumption on itertools.combinations (C(m, n-1) subsets, Theta(n) each to generate, build, search and weigh; PROOFS.md, section 6)

algorithms.name: Kruskal with union-find
algorithms.time_complexity: Omega(n^2 log n) in the worst case if sorted() is a deterministic comparison sort and O(n^2 log n) if it runs in O(m log m) worst-case time (both background assumptions): for every n some weight assignment of K_n makes sorted() perform at least log2(m!) comparisons (decision-tree argument, under the machine-model assumption that sorted() is deterministic and learns about the keys only from < comparisons); the rest of the work is O(m log n), since union by size keeps every union-find tree of height at most log2 n. PROOFS.md, section 6.

algorithms.name: Prim, array version
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) on K_n (n-1 rounds, two Theta(n) scans each), linear in the input size (PROOFS.md, section 6)

algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(3^n) on every input: exactly 3^n calls (n >= 0) and (3^(n-1) - 1)/2 cost comparisons (n >= 1)

algorithms.name: cubic interval DP (every root)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) on every input: n(n+1)(n+2)/6 candidate roots, (n+1)n(n-1)/6 cost comparisons

algorithms.name: Knuth's speed-up (monotone roots)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) on every input. Upper bound: for each length L >= 2 the range widths telescope, sum_i (r[i+1][i+L] - r[i][i+L-1] + 1) = (n - L + 1) + r[n-L+1][n] - r[0][L-1] <= 2n - L; lower bound: n(n-1)/2 intervals of length >= 2, each evaluating at least one candidate. entries.title: Weighted perfect matchings of planar grid graphs (dimers): backtracking enumeration vs Kasteleyn's signed determinant (Bareiss)

algorithms.name: backtracking enumeration of perfect matchings
algorithms.time_complexity: O(N 2^(N/2)) on every instance (PROOFS.md, section 5): the search tree has branching factor <= 2 and depth <= N/2, and the scan for the next unmatched vertex only moves forward along a root-to-leaf path. The time is also at least the number of perfect matchings, which is exponential in N for unit weights: F(N/2 + 1) = Theta(phi^(N/2)) (Fibonacci numbers) on the (N/2) x 2 ladder, and at least 2^(N/4) on a x b grids with a and b even (N/4 disjoint 2 x 2 blocks with 2 tilings each). Counted cost (one multiplication weight * subtotal per search-tree edge) on the V2 family, the unit-weight (n/2) x 2 ladder: Theta(phi^(n/2)) = Theta(1.272^n), exactly L(n/2 + 2) - 3 = phi^(n/2+2) + (-1/phi)^(n/2+2) - 3 multiplications (L = Lucas numbers). On the 2 x (n/2) ladder (the same graph, vertices numbered along the long side) it is Theta(n phi^(n/2)), see caveats.

algorithms.name: Kasteleyn signed determinant with Bareiss fraction-free elimination
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(N^3) arithmetic operations: exactly (m-1) m (2m-1)/2 = (N-2) N (N-1)/8 multiplications and exact divisions (m = N/2) on every instance with a non-zero answer, whatever row swaps occur (the loops do not depend on the values unless a column is zero from the pivot down, which forces det = 0); at most that many when the answer is 0, none for odd N; plus Theta(N^2) entry reads and negations to build K. The integers are not of constant size: every Bareiss value is a minor of K (rows permuted), at most (2 w_max)^(N/2) in absolute value by Hadamard's inequality (each row of K has at most 4 non-zero entries, so Euclidean norm <= 2 w_max), and a product before division is at most 2 (2 w_max)^N in absolute value, so all values have O(N log(2 w_max)) bits. Bit complexity O(N^3 M(N log(2 w_max))), where M(b) bounds the cost of one multiplication or exact division of b-bit integers (O(b^2) with schoolbook arithmetic, which gives O(N^5 log^2(2 w_max))): polynomial in the input size (PROOFS.md, sections 4 and 7).

entries.title: Regular-expression matching: backtracking vs memoised backtracking vs Thompson's NFA simulation

algorithms.name: backtracking (consume first)
algorithms.time_complexity: Exponential in the worst case. On P_n exactly (n + 2) * 2^(n-1) - 1 symbol-character comparisons, Theta(n * 2^n). In general O(2^(m + |t|)): every call makes at most two recursive calls and each increases i + j, so the call tree has depth <= m + |t| + 1.

algorithms.name: memoised backtracking
algorithms.time_complexity: O((m + 1)(|t| + 1)) subproblems with O(1) work each (O(1) dictionary operations, each counted as one step), i.e. O(n^2) for the stated n. On P_n exactly n(n + 1) symbol-character comparisons, Theta(n^2).

algorithms.name: Thompson's NFA simulation
algorithms.time_complexity: O((m + 1)(|t| + 1)): at most m + 1 states per step with O(1) work each, plus an O(m + 1) closure per step; O(n^2) for the stated n. On P_n exactly n(n + 1) symbol-character comparisons, Theta(n^2).

entries.title: Single-pair shortest path: simple-path enumeration vs Dijkstra

algorithms.name: simple-path enumeration
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n (n-2)!) on every n x n input: exactly 2P calls of the search with P = floor(e (n-2)!) (n >= 3), the number of simple s-t paths of the complete digraph, and n neighbour checks at each of the P calls not at t (PROOFS.md, section 2)

algorithms.name: Dijkstra (array version)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) with an array (linear in the n x n weight-matrix input; it reads exactly n(n-1)/2 distinct weights, for each pair of vertices the one leaving the vertex settled first), which is optimal up to a constant factor for weight-matrix input: for n >= 4 split the n - 2 vertices other than s, t into U (floor((n-2)/2) of them) and X, and set w(s, u) = 1, w(u, x) = 2 and w(x, t) = 1 for u in U, x in X, all other weights 100; then dist(s, t) = 4, and lowering any one weight w(u, x) to 1 makes it 3, so on this instance every correct deterministic algorithm (and every run of a zero-error randomized one, with its random bits fixed) reads all floor((n-2)^2/4) weights w(u, x), in the model where each step reads at most one entry and the steps depend only on the values read. PROOFS.md, sections 4 and 5. (Heap-based versions are background, not implemented.)

entries.title: Counting spanning trees: edge-subset enumeration vs Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem (Bareiss)

algorithms.name: enumeration of all (n-1)-edge subsets
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n^2 + n log n C(m, n-1)) under the background itertools assumption and Omega(n^2 + n C(m, n-1)): Theta(n^2) to read the matrix, plus C(m, n-1) subsets, each generated by itertools.combinations in O(n) (background), at Theta(n) each to reset the union-find arrays and at most n-1 unions (2(n-1) finds of O(log n) each, because union by size keeps every tree of height at most log2 n; PROOFS.md, section 4). C(m, n-1) is non-decreasing in m, so these bounds are largest on K_n, m = n(n-1)/2: (n/2)^(n-1) <= C(n(n-1)/2, n-1) <= (e n/2)^(n-1), i.e. 2^Theta(n log n), super-exponential in n (PROOFS.md, section 1).

algorithms.name: Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem with Bareiss fraction-free elimination
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) arithmetic operations: exactly (n-2)(n-1)(2n-3)/2 multiplications and exact divisions on every connected graph (no zero pivot occurs), at most that many otherwise (it stops at the first zero pivot), plus Theta(n^2) additions to build the Laplacian. The integers are not of constant size: every intermediate entry is a minor of the reduced Laplacian, of absolute value < n^(n-1) by Hadamard's inequality (each row has Euclidean norm <= sqrt(n(n-1)) < n), and a product before division is < 2 n^(2(n-1)), so all values have O(n log n) bits. Bit complexity O(n^3 M(n log n)), where M(b) bounds the cost of one multiplication or exact division of b-bit integers (O(n^5 log^2 n) with schoolbook arithmetic): polynomial in the n^2-bit input (PROOFS.md, sections 2, 6 and 7).

entries.title: Maximum bipartite matching: one augmenting path per vertex (Kuhn) vs Hopcroft-Karp

algorithms.name: Kuhn's augmenting paths (one DFS per left vertex)
algorithms.time_complexity: O(V (V + E)), i.e. O(V E) when E = Omega(V): one O(V + E) search per left vertex, and at most n_left E <= V E edge scans on every input (in one search a left vertex is pushed at most once, since the root is free and every other pushed vertex is the partner of a right vertex seen for the first time, and a pushed vertex reads each entry of its list at most once). On the adversarial family G_k (V = 4k^2 + k, E = 2k^4 + k^2) exactly (7k^6 + 9k^4 + 11k^2 - 3k)/6 edge scans for every k >= 1. Proof sketch, with a = k^2: before gadget root u < a, gadget left vertex i is matched to right vertex u - 1 - i (i < u), so the search from u runs through all u matched gadget vertices, reads (u + 1)(u + 2)/2 entries and succeeds; each of the other a gadget roots fails after reading a(a + 1) entries (its own list and the lists of the a matched gadget vertices); in path j the roots L_2..L_j read 1 entry each and L_1 reads 2j - 1, so path j costs 3j - 2. The sum C(a + 2, 3) + a^2 (a + 1) + k(3k - 1)/2 is the formula, and it equals the V2 counts listed under verification. So Kuhn makes Theta(V E) = Theta(V^3) scans on G_k; the ratio to V E tends to 7/48 (complete proofs: PROOFS.md sections 1, 2, 8 and 9)

algorithms.name: Hopcroft-Karp
algorithms.time_complexity: O((V + E) sqrt(V)): fewer than sqrt(2V) + 1 phases for V >= 1, O(V + E) each (PROOFS.md section 7, Theorem HK; credit: Hopcroft & Karp 1973); O(V^2.5) on dense graphs (the paper's title bound). On the adversarial family G_k exactly k + 1 phases (k augmenting phases and a final search that finds no augmenting path) and (24k^5 + 9k^4 + 4k^3 + 24k^2 - 25k + 12)/6 = Theta(E sqrt V) edge scans for every k >= 1; the ratio to E sqrt V tends to 1. Proof sketch, with a = k^2: in phase 1 the breadth-first search reads all E entries, and the depth-first searches read a(a + 1)/2 + a^2 + k(k + 1)/2 entries, match all a gadget right vertices and path 1, and leave path j >= 2 with the j - 1 edges L_i R_(i-1) matched and L_1, R_j free; in phase t (2 <= t <= k) the target level is t, the breadth-first search reads 2a^2 entries in the gadget and 2t - 1 in each path j >= t, and the depth-first searches read 2a^2 in the gadget, 2t - 1 in path t, which they repair, and 2t + 1 in each later path, which they leave unchanged; phase k + 1 reads 2a^2 entries and finds no free right vertex. The per-phase counts sum to the formula, which equals the V2 counts listed under verification (complete proof: PROOFS.md section 3)

entries.title: Multi-pattern string matching: naive matching per pattern vs KMP per pattern vs Aho-Corasick

algorithms.name: naive matching per pattern
algorithms.time_complexity: O(N L) character comparisons; Theta(sum over patterns of max(N - m + 1, 0) m) in the worst case. On the V2 family exactly sum_j j (n^2 - j + 1) = n(n+1)(3n^2 - 2n + 2)/6 comparisons = Theta(n^4) (each of the n^2 - j + 1 alignments of a^(j-1) b matches j - 1 characters and fails on the b).

algorithms.name: Knuth-Morris-Pratt per pattern
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(P N + L) time on every input with P >= 1, and Theta(P N + L) comparisons whenever N >= 1 (between P N + L - P and 3 P N + 3(L - P); with an empty text and patterns of length 1 nothing is compared): Theta(N + m) per pattern (at most 3(m - 1) comparisons for the failure table and 3N for the scan, at least m - 1 and N: the implementation compares the current character again after the while loop, as in string-matching-naive-vs-kmp). On the V2 family exactly 3n^3 - 2n^2 - 5n + 6 comparisons for n >= 2 = Theta(n^3): pattern b costs N, pattern ab costs 2N, and a^(j-1) b for j >= 3 costs 3j - 6 (failure table) + 3N - j (scan), with N = n^2.

algorithms.name: Aho-Corasick
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(N + L) character comparisons for P >= 1 and a fixed alphabet of sigma characters, O(N + L) for every P (children kept as lists scanned linearly, at most sigma comparisons per lookup; at most 2N lookups in the scan and at most 3L in the construction, L for the trie and 2L for the failure links; at least N + L - sigma comparisons when P >= 1 (with no patterns nothing is compared), since every scan step ends with a lookup in a non-empty child list, at most T of the L insertion lookups find an empty list (T = number of trie nodes created), and every created node of depth >= 2 ends its failure-link search with a lookup in a non-empty list), independent of the number of occurrences. On the V2 family exactly 4n^2 - 3 comparisons for n >= 1 = Theta(n^2): (n-1)^2 to build the trie (inserting a^(j-1) b costs 2(j-2) + 1 comparisons for j >= 2, 0 for j = 1), 3n - 5 for the failure links (n >= 2: 1 for the b-child and 2 for the a-child of every a^d, d = 1..n-1, the a-child only for d <= n-2), and 3n^2 - n + 1 for the scan (n >= 2; 2 per character down the a-chain for the first n - 1 characters, then 3 per character: the b-only node a^(n-1) fails, its failure link a^(n-2) has the a-child at the second position).

entries.title: 3XOR: all triples vs a Patricia trie (deterministic quadratic)

algorithms.name: all triples
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) in the worst case. Exactly, on every instance without a solution (the V2 family is one): C(n, 2) XORs and C(n, 3) equality tests, C(n, 2) + C(n, 3) = C(n + 1, 3) = (n^3 - n)/6 word operations (the middle loop runs once per pair, the inner loop once per triple; Pascal's rule sums the two binomials). With a solution it stops at the first hit (PROOFS.md sections 1 and 3).

algorithms.name: Patricia trie
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n^2 + n w) word operations; Theta(n^2) in the worst case when log2(n) + 1 <= w = O(n) (n distinct odd-weight words exist there and form a no-instance whose n rounds make n XORs each; exact count on the V2 family). The zero scan is n comparisons, the build at most n w bit tests (each index is tested once per bit until its group is a singleton), and each of the |D| <= n rounds costs O(|D|): |D| - 1 bit tests at branching nodes, |D| XORs and a merge of at most 2|D| - 1 steps. Exactly, on the V2 family (all w-bit words of odd Hamming weight, n = 2^(w-1), no solution): 7n^2 + 2n log2(n) - 3n operations. Derivation: n zero comparisons; the build tests every word once at each of the bits w-1..1 (a group fixed on its top bits holds all suffixes of one parity, 2^(r-1) words for r remaining bits, and splits at the next bit while r >= 2; at r = 1 it is a single word), n(w - 1) = n log2(n) bit tests of 2 operations each (AND, truth test), and the trie has n leaves and n - 1 branching nodes; per a: 2(n - 1) for the bit tests at branching nodes, n XORs, and the merge: {a XOR x} is the set of even-weight words, which interleaves with the odd-weight words (each pair 2t, 2t + 1 holds one of each), so the merge consumes every word up to 2^w - 2, 2n - 1 steps of one equality test and one less-than test, 4n - 2; per a 7n - 4. Total n + 2n log2(n) + n(7n - 4). Complete proofs: PROOFS.md sections 2 and 5 (on every input at most n + 2nw + 7n^2 counted operations).

On the V2 family (m = k, item i matched by rules i and i+1 mod k) exactly k! (k+1)(k+3)/3 - 1 counted operations (k >= 2) = Theta(k! k^2) = Theta(k! k m): k! k(k+1)/3 truth tests (the earlier of an item's two rules stands on average at position (k+1)/3 of a random order: P(min >= j) = C(k-j+1, 2)/C(k, 2), summed over j = 1..k this is C(k+1, 3)/C(k, 2)), k! k additions and k! - 1 comparisons (none for the first order).

algorithms.name: dynamic programming over subsets of rules

Exactly 3k^2 + (7k - 2) 2^(k-1) + 2 counted operations on the V2 family (k >= 2): 3km = 3k^2 for building the rule lists (k truth tests per item) and the masks (k shifts and k additions per item); 2k 2^k for the capture tests (an & and a truth test per item and subset); k 2^(k-1) gain additions (each item is uncaptured for the 2^(k-2) subsets avoiding its two rules and then adds 2 costs); k 2^(k-1) transition additions; k 2^(k-1) - 2^k + 1 comparisons (a subset T is reached |T| times, the first arrival is stored without comparison); 1 final addition.

entries.title: Bernstein-Vazirani: n classical queries vs 1 quantum query

lower_bounds.bound: n queries for every success probability > 1/2, randomized algorithms included
lower_bounds.source: Proved in this entry (PROOFS.md §4): for a uniformly random s, the answers s.x_1, ..., s.x_q to q queries (chosen adaptively) leave s uniform on the solutions of q linear equations over GF(2), an affine subspace of dimension >= n - q, so a deterministic q-query algorithm outputs s with probability at most 2^(q-n). Averaging over its coins, every randomized q-query algorithm also succeeds with probability at most 2^(q-n) on average over s, hence on some s; success > 1/2 on every s therefore needs q >= n. The problem is from Bernstein & Vazirani 1997

algorithms.name: classical: query the unit vectors
algorithms.time_complexity: n queries (optimal classically, also for randomized algorithms that succeed with probability > 1/2; PROOFS.md §1, §4)

algorithms.name: Bernstein-Vazirani quantum algorithm
algorithms.time_complexity: 1 query (O(n) gates besides the oracle)

entries.title: Collision problem: Theta(N^(1/2)) classical queries vs O(N^(1/3)) quantum queries (Brassard-Hoyer-Tapp)

lower_bounds.bound: Omega(sqrt N) = Omega(2^(n/2)) queries for bounded error (more than sqrt(N)/2 queries for success probability 1/2 on every input, N >= 16)
lower_bounds.source: Proved in this entry (PROOFS.md §6), by the birthday argument: on a uniformly random 2-to-1 function, after i collision-free queries ANY next query completes a pair with probability exactly i/(N-i), so q queries reveal a collision with probability at most q^2/(2(N-q)), and guessing an unseen pair succeeds with probability at most 1/(N-q-1); averaging over the coins gives the randomized bound. Stated as the classical optimum (expected Theta(sqrt N)) in the arXiv note of Brassard, Hoyer & Tapp (1997). It also follows from the classical lower bound for Simon's problem (simon-classical-vs-quantum), because every Simon instance is 2-to-1 and any collision reveals s.

lower_bounds.bound: N/2 + 1 queries in the worst case for algorithms that are always correct (N >= 4)
lower_bounds.source: Proved in this entry (PROOFS.md §6 and §1), by an adversary argument: answer the first N/2 queries with distinct values; a 2-to-1 function consistent with these answers can always avoid pairing the two output points, so no pair is certain. Pigeonhole makes N/2 + 1 sufficient.

algorithms.name: classical birthday search
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(sqrt N) = Theta(2^(n/2)) queries expected: E[Q] = sum_{q>=0} prod_{i=1}^{q-1} (N-2i)/(N-i) = 2^N / binom(N, N/2), which lies strictly between sqrt(pi N / 2) and sqrt(pi N / 2) e^(1/(3N)), so E[Q] ~ sqrt(pi N / 2) (PROOFS.md §4); at most N/2 + 1

algorithms.name: Brassard-Hoyer-Tapp, known number of marked points
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(N^(1/3)) = Theta(2^(n/3)) queries expected on every input (PROOFS.md §5): exactly k if K contains a collision, and k + (2m + 1)/sin^2((2m+1) theta) otherwise, with sin^2 theta = k/N and m = floor(pi/(4 theta)), counting 2 queries per Grover iteration; over the harness's random 2-to-1 functions k + P_nc(k) (2m + 1)/sin^2((2m+1) theta), P_nc(k) = prod_{i=1}^{k-1} (N-2i)/(N-i) the probability that K contains no collision; between 2.564 and 2.572 N^(1/3) at n = 15, 18, ..., 30 (experiment Part C) and between 2.536 and 2.572 N^(1/3) at every n = 15..30 (exact evaluation of this formula)

algorithms.name: Brassard-Hoyer-Tapp with BBHT exponential search (unknown number of marked points)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(N^(1/3)) queries expected on every input: k + P_nc(k) (2 I(k) + C(k)), where I(k) < 9 sqrt(N/k) and C(k) < log_{6/5} sqrt(N) + 5 are the expected Grover iterations and rounds of the exponential search (PROOFS.md §5, with Theorem E of the minimum-finding proofs; credit: BBHT Theorem 3, O(sqrt(N/t)) iterations for t marked items); exact expectation between 3.844 and 3.897 N^(1/3) at every n = 18..30 (exact evaluation; experiment Part C at n = 18, 21, ..., 30); no limit is proved

entries.title: Deutsch-Jozsa: 2^(n-1)+1 exact classical queries vs 1 exact quantum query (no gap once classical error is allowed)

lower_bounds.bound: 2^(n-1) + 1 queries in the worst case, for any algorithm that is always correct
lower_bounds.setting: query (oracle) model, EXACT (zero-error) computation, unconditional. The same argument forces 2^(n-1) + 1 queries on every constant input for zero-error randomized (Las Vegas) algorithms. It does NOT hold for bounded-error randomized algorithms, which need only O(1) queries (see the randomized algorithm in this entry).
lower_bounds.source: Proved in this entry (PROOFS.md §6), by an adversary argument: answer f(x) = 0 to the first 2^(n-1) distinct queries; both the constant-0 function and a balanced function (ones on unqueried points only) remain consistent, so no exact algorithm can stop.

algorithms.time_complexity: 2^(n-1) + 1 queries in the worst case (optimal for exact classical algorithms; PROOFS.md §1, §6); exactly 3 - 4/(N + 2) queries on average over uniformly random balanced functions (N = 2^n), so at most 3 and tending to 3 as n grows: the first j values agree with probability 2 prod_{i<j} (N/2 - i)/(N - i) <= 2^(1-j), and the expected number of queries is 1 plus the sum of these probabilities over j >= 1 (PROOFS.md §5)

bases: Moran–Schwartz–Yuan 2026, arXiv:2602.13171
provenance.pending_note: Moran, Schwartz and Yuan (2026, §3.2) state the result for a ⟨2,4,5,32⟩ ℤ[1/2] scheme that they attribute to Hopcroft and Kerr (1971), and for Smirnov's ⟨3,3,6,40⟩ ℤ[1/2] scheme. They print neither scheme and identify no files. No source checked supports a rank-32 Hopcroft–Kerr scheme for ⟨2,4,5⟩ (by the abstract of Hopcroft and Kerr (1971), their construction multiplies a 4×2 by a 2×5 matrix, the format corresponding to ⟨2,4,5⟩ under the permutation symmetry of formats, with 33 multiplications), and the pinned ⟨3,3,6;40⟩ file is attributed to Smirnov but not compared with his paper. The evidence (the ring ℤ[1/2] and the trace properties they describe hold for both pinned files) points to the pinned files but does not establish that their statements concern them or schemes equivalent to them. This note proves the statement for the pinned files.
